The call names nodes B and F, outlined in the accent color; after it both read 7, while the other four nodes keep their values." width="100%"} Writes a single named attribute onto nodes, modifying the graph in place. The same value can be broadcast to many nodes, or different values can be supplied per node via a list (paired by position) or a dict (keyed by node). The attribute is created if it doesn't exist and overwritten if it does; all other attributes are left alone. This is the main way to attach data to nodes after they have been created, for example: - storing externally computed scores or classifications (e.g., from a model or a CSV) - tagging a known set of nodes with a category or flag - setting visual attributes such as `color` or `size` before plotting The `values=` dict form pairs naturally with methods that return `{node_id: value}` dictionaries (such as the `return_dict=True` mode of centrality measures). To set attributes on the current selection instead of on an explicit list, see `set_node_attrs_ws()`. ::: ## Parameters {.doc-parameters} ::: {.doc-definition-items} [node_attr]{.doc-parameter-name}[:]{.doc-parameter-annotation-sep} [str]{.doc-parameter-annotation} : The name of the attribute to set (e.g., `"color"`, `"score"`). This becomes a column of the same name in `get_node_df()`. [values]{.doc-parameter-name}[:]{.doc-parameter-annotation-sep} [Any | list[Any] | dict[int, Any]]{.doc-parameter-annotation} : The value(s) to write. Three forms are accepted: - a **dict** mapping node IDs or labels to values. Only nodes that appear both in the dict and in `nodes=` (all nodes, by default) are updated; nodes missing from the dict are left unchanged. - a **list** of values paired by position with `nodes=`. The list length must equal the number of target nodes. When `nodes=` is `None` the pairing follows the internal order of `get_node_ids()`, which is not necessarily insertion order, so pass `nodes=` explicitly when using a list. - **any other value** (a string, number, tuple, `None`, etc.), which is written to every target node. [nodes]{.doc-parameter-name}[:]{.doc-parameter-annotation-sep} [list[int | str] | None]{.doc-parameter-annotation} [=]{.doc-parameter-default-sep .op} [None]{.doc-parameter-default} : The nodes to update, given as node IDs (`int`) or labels (`str`), which may be mixed. If `None` (the default), all nodes in the graph are targeted. Labels are resolved to IDs, and an unknown label raises a `ValueError`. ::: ## Returns {.doc-returns} ::: {.doc-definition-items} [Graph]{.doc-parameter-annotation} : Self for method chaining. ::: ## Raises {.doc-raises} ::: {.doc-definition-items} [ValueError]{.doc-parameter-annotation} : If `values=` is a list whose length doesn't match the number of target nodes, or if a label given in `nodes=` (or as a dict key) does not exist in the graph. ::: ## Examples {.doc-examples} Passing a single value applies it to every node listed in `nodes=`; node `C` is not listed, so it doesn't get a `color` entry at all: ::: {#fd9a519b .cell execution_count=1} ``` {.python .cell-code} import edgecase as ec graph = ( ec.Graph() .add_nodes(["A", "B", "C"]) ) a_id = graph.get_id_from_label("A") b_id = graph.get_id_from_label("B") graph.set_node_attrs("color", "blue", nodes=[a_id, b_id]) graph.get_node_attrs("color") ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=1} ``` {2: 'blue', 1: 'blue'} ``` ::: ::: Omitting `nodes=` entirely applies the value to every node in the graph: ::: {#83c5d592 .cell execution_count=2} ``` {.python .cell-code} graph.set_node_attrs("status", "active") graph.get_node_attrs("status") ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=2} ``` {2: 'active', 3: 'active', 1: 'active'} ``` ::: ::: A list assigns a different value to each node, paired up by position with `nodes=`. Labels work just as well as IDs here: ::: {#250dc376 .cell execution_count=3} ``` {.python .cell-code} graph.set_node_attrs("score", [100, 85, 92], nodes=["A", "B", "C"]) graph.get_node_attrs("score") ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=3} ``` {2: 85, 3: 92, 1: 100} ``` ::: ::: A dict is the most explicit form, mapping each node directly to its own value. Keys may be labels or IDs, and nodes left out of the dict (here `B`) are untouched, so `B` keeps its earlier score of `85`: ::: {#e89f801d .cell execution_count=4} ``` {.python .cell-code} graph.set_node_attrs("score", {"A": 60, "C": 75}) graph.get_node_attrs("score") ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=4} ``` {2: 85, 3: 75, 1: 60} ``` ::: :::
